Leadership for the Counsellor 


by Mrs. Ralph Raymer 
Camp Tanamakoon 

Leadership for Counsellors is a vast 
topic. Obviously, we cannot condense it 
all into one hour. 

The sub-title for this session on 
leadership reads “how lo develop your 
full leadership potential”. It sounds as 
though you come in here and get a magic 
incantation which will produce phenom¬ 
enal results. Since this is the assignment, 
we shall try to produce a do-it-yourself- 
kit for making-the-most-of-your-leadership 
ability. 

Thought and Action 

The only way.I can see to develop any 
portion of one’s make-up is through 
intelligent linking of Thought and Action. 
Because you are a human being you 
possess the capacity to Think and 
Reason and influence your own behaviour. 
If there is one single personal attribute 
I would exhort, beg, and beseech you to 
use to full capacity as the program 
states, it is your ability to think. This 
do-it-yourself kit will consist of a series 
of questions. You will ask them of 
yourself and you will THINK to obtain 
the answers. I shall start by clarifying 
the term counsellor as I am going to use 
it now. A camp counsellor is an official 
leader in any camp whose work involves 
associating with and working with 
campers-no matter what the name of the 
job may be in any particular camp. 

Some Questions 

The first do-it-yourself question is 
WHY? Why do you wish to be a coun¬ 
sellor? Examine your motives. If you are 
gping to be a genuine leader you must 
eventually be able to answer that ques¬ 
tion-why? Examine your motives with 
honesty. If the purely selfish ones 


outweigh the truly unselfish ones, you 
may be unhappy and badly adjusted in an 
environment which is dominated by 
people and their very human needs and 
characteristics. To be quite fair, I must 
add that all of you already possess a 
deep fund of knowledge about leadership 
and about camp. The very fact that you 
are here this moment means that you have 
been favourably conditioned. It is your 
job and mine to bring this knowledge to 
the surface. 

The second question to ask yourself 
is-“What kind of a leader do I want to 
be?” Leaders of all kinds have existed 
throughout the ages and will continue to 
arise; the world needs leaders. Few of 
us are destined to be the spectacular 
leader who streaks like a meteor through 
the sky, but we can do the best with what 
we’ve got. Fundamental to the kind of 
leader you are going to be is considera¬ 
tion of what kind of leaders are needed 
in Camps today, and what kind of a 
leader is needed by the children in your 
care? The answers to these questions 
need more than superficial thinking... 
This is a profound area. 

Let us get to work on creating YOUR 
IMAGE AS A LEADER. Since most 
people get their first impressions of a 
new leader through their eyes, ask 
yourself “How do I look?” Do you appear 
clean, dirty, tidy, disheveled, alert, 
half-asleep, upright, a slouch, friendly, 
forbidding, suitably or unsuitably 
dressed, and on and on. Take a good 
look at yourself. Your appearance speaks; 
sometimes it shouts or screams. Your 
appearance creates an impression and 
broadcasts a message. Try hard to look 
like a leader. 


92 


Canadian Camping 



Next question: HOW DO YOU SOUND? 
Listen to yourself: Do you speak to 
others as you would wish them to speak 
to you? Are the sounds you make inter¬ 
preted as friendly, aloof, well-educated, 
like a dropout, interested, bored, rude, 
polite, tough, gentle, confident or scared? 
Do you holler and shriek, or just barely 
whisper? How do you sound? How should 
you sound? Don’t laugh-every public 
personality from politics to TV gives 
much serious consideration to this point. 

Next question. HOW DO YOU ACT? 
Human beings are reasoning creatures, 
they observe and draw conclusions. 
Campers do this. They look and they 
experience your presence and they decide 
whether or not they wish to follow you. 
Do you act like a friend? Do you help in 
time of trouble? What kind of an example 
do you set? Children make judgements! 
But one endearing quality of most 
children is that they are ready to accept 
you as their leader if you look and sound 
and act like a leader. Don’t drive them 
away! 

Tools of Leadership 

Now you will need some TOOLS of 
leadership. First let us THINK on the 
subject of CAUSE and EFFECT. Cause 
and Effect are fundamental in human 
relations and in understanding human 
behaviour—and in predicting usual 
behaviour. Ask yourselves “If I do this 
what will happen?” A skilled teacher 
employs Cause and Effect constantly. He 
experiments with methods and materials 
and learns how to teach to get the best 
results. 

One of the things one experiences and 
observes at camp is Group Behaviour. 
From practical experience, I have formed 
a few working rules about controlling 
group behaviour. 

First-let the campers know ahead of 
time. 

Second-keep the campers interested. 


Letting the campers know ahead of 
time involves thinking ahead of campers. 
In other words, always plan ahead. There 
are various methods of giving advance 
notice. The most obvious is by RULES. 
Camp rules should be taught to the 
campers as soon as they arrive. Rules 
should be easy to understand, and, they 
must be logical. Rules should be few in 
number and confined to important areas 
such as Safety. But Rules are most 
assuredly not the magic key to group 
control. 

The effect of presenting a well- 
planned program is an interested co-opera¬ 
tive group having fun. Any skillful leader 
gives evidence of advance planning. He 
is aware of every detail. Make use of 
every opportunity you have to observe 
leaders in action. Make mental notes 
about what methods succeed and what 
fail. It is very useful to know what won’t 
work as well as what will work. Follow 
the same procedure through all your 
duties. Treat your cabin group as a 
group, plan for the group and observe 
results. Let the group know what is 
expected of it, and keep it busy and 
fascinated. From its reactions, you can 
learn how to plan in the future. In 
almost every instance, when trouble 
arises it is caused by lack of leadership 
on the part of the counsellor. A knowl¬ 
edgeable leader senses potential trouble 
areas and approaches his group with the 
planning ahead idea. The thinking leader 
talks with his group and learns its 
interests, its temperament and abilities. 
He creates, in the minds of those children, 
a feeling that time is precious and to be 
used to advantage. 

There will be times when a group 
activity turns out to be a real lesson in 
frustrating confusion. Sit down afterwards 
and think. Ask yourself why , analyse and 
evaluate and find out what went wrong 
and how to avoid it next time. Ask 


Summer, 1968 


93 


yourself—“How can I foresee this in the 
future? What part of the responsibility 
was mine?” and finally, “What can I do 
about it?” 

The Individual Child 

Now we must speak about the indi¬ 
vidual child. You know that consideration 
for the human individual is important. 
You are the most important person in your 
world, and each child has a world of 
which he is the centre. As you grow in 
maturity, you learn how to co-ordinate 
your individual world with the worlds of 
others. Children have not yet reached 
your level. Remember that each child is 
a constantly changing person in a 
constantly changing pattern. 

Here are some simple effective tools 
to help in dealing with individuals. First 
—learn names and use them constantly. 
Second-keep your eyes open, your mouth 
closed and observe. Learn and accept 
the fact that children are not alike and 


they are most certainly not average. 
Every single item you observe is teach¬ 
ing you something about an individual 
child. Third: now give each individual 
some thought. Total up your observations. 
Think, what is this child like? Think, 
what can I do to help this child? Love 
and encourage every child. 

All children have a few unwritten 
iron-clad rules they expect their leaders 
to obey, and they are bitterly disap¬ 
pointed when leaders, break these rules. 
Here are the childrens rules: 1. Always 
be fair. 2. Never play favourites. 3. Be 
consistent. 4. Be a good example. 5. Be 
fun. 6. Be kind. 

“Discipline” seems to worry young 
counsellors. If I had to make one general 
rule about discipline, I would say “When 
you see something that you know is 
wrong or is going to create a problem, 
take immediate action”. Be fair, con¬ 
sistent and kind, but take action.

Another bit of advice: work with children, 
play with them, talk with them, but don’t 
act like them. The counsellor who acts 
like a camper loses the respect of the 
group. A few words about popularity. 
Strangely enough, popularity and effective 
leadership do not go hand in hand. A 
very poor leader, a weak person, an evil 
person can be very popular. My advice is 
“Don’t try to be popular and don’t use 
popularity as a measuring device”. It is 
a false value. 

We—not I 

And now the final steps in this Do-It- 
Yourself Kit. We must now assemble all 
the pieces to produce the finished prod¬ 
uct. When you get to camp you are no 
longer an I but part of a great big WE. 
At camp, the question is what are WE 
trying to accomplish and how are WE 
going to do it? If WE are going to 
accomplish great things, challenge these 
children, imbue them with lasting values, 
teach them to treasure the wonders of 
Nature, WE have to do it together. WE 
translate philosophy into a vital experi¬ 
ence for children. To become a part of 
this great big WE, you do not have to 
lose your individuality; the variety of 
personalities and talents, within the 
group, increases its colour and its effec- 
tiveness-so long as the individuals are 
united in a common purpose. 

Ask yourself-is this an I or a WE 
project? Again the admonition is THINK. 
When you are tempted to neglect a duty- 
THINK. When you are planning your 
work-THINK. What can I do to help make 
the philosophy of this Camp meaningful 
and rich? If you are going to develop your 
full capacity as a Counsellor, you are 
going to aim at lofty targets. One never 
learns all about Camping and groups, and 
above all, about children. But if you need 
incentive to keep on striving to be a 
wonderful leader, THINK. THINK of the 
material you are working for and with, our 
nation’s most precious asset, our chil¬ 


dren. It is a great and sacred privilege 
to work with children. You are working 
with the future-you are helping to mold 
and direct tomorrow’s world. I close with 
an earnest behest...if you are going to 
be a Counsellor—be a Good Counsellor. 

(The above is a very condensed version 
of Mrs. Raymef s talk to the 1967 Ontario 
Camping Association Conference held at 
the Inn-on-the-Park, Toronto , Ontario.) 


Ottawa 

canoeing course 

From June 22-29 at the Camp of the 
University of Ottawa, some seventy miles 
north of Ottawa, the second Canoeing 
Instructor Course, sanctioned by the 
Canadian Camping Association, will be 
held. 

Again Professor Kirk A.W. Wipper of 
the University of Toronto will be the 
guest specialist and Professor Claude 
Cousineau of the University of Ottawa 
will act as director of the course. 

The course content is presented in 
the form of lecture, seminar, film, prac¬ 
tical session and teaching practices. It 
includes: stroke analysis, teaching, 
organization of canoeing program in 
camp, safety, history of Canadian 
canoes, canoe tripping, rapids shooting 
and canoe racing. 

Further information and application 
forms can be obtained by writing to the 
School of Physical Education and 
Recreation, University of Ottawa, Ottawa 
2, Ontario. The fee is $75.00. 

The outstanding success of last 
year’s course augurs well for this one.

AQUATIC CALCULATIONS 

By Kirk A.W. I Vipper 


As the summer camping season 
rapidly approaches, thoughts of adven¬ 
turous activities especially in, on and 
around our waterways come to our minds. 
Our campers too, are looking forward to 
long cool plunges on hot summer days, 
to the excitement of manoeuvring a 
sailboat in unpredictable breezes, to the 
skimming around a bend in a river on a 
canoe trip, to the exploration of the 
underwater world in skin diving, to the 
swift response of a sleek kayak, to the 
exhilaration of a water ski turn, or to any 
of the other fun filled water activities 
that are possible and available. All of 
the above are activities with a significant 
purpose but each also involves a risk. 
Of course that risk can be calculated and 
intelligent measures can be taken to cope 
in such a way that safety is ensured 
without detracting appreciably from the 
adventure of the activity. The purpose 
of this brief article is to review some of 
the special areas which deserve recon¬ 
sideration. 

1.Guards —How well prepared are they 
for their job? Much can be said about 
waterfront patrols, their attitudes, and 
their training. Regardless of the qualifi¬ 
cations they bring however, it is the 
writer’s opinion that at least the follow¬ 
ing three steps should be taken when 
they arrive at camp. 

1) Drill-practise techniques and pro¬ 
cedures specific to your waterfront 
requirements. 

2) Test-examine the guards to renew 
their formal qualifications. 

3) Recognize-give your guards a bonus 
or some special privilege in recognition 
of their extra effort (time off, etc.). 


2. Checking systems —Do they still 
work? Are they consistent for all water¬ 
front activities? 

If the system you have adopted is 
sluggish and evokes a poor response 
from campers and staff, a re-evaluation 
is essential. After all, if a real emer¬ 
gency does exist, only a limited number 
of seconds can be allowed in a check 
and rescue. Furthermore, a checking 
system must apply to all waterfront 
activities; swimming, diving, canoeing, 
kayaking, sailing, water skiing, skin 
diving and so on. This total approach 
will tend to reinforce with campers and 
staff an attitude of a sensible precaution 
in reference to hazardous activity. There 
is a degree of risk in all aquatic pursuits. 

3. Search plans-Is there an acceptable, 
sensible search system? Has it been 
practised? Are the procedures clear to 
all for exceptional circumstances such 
as staff days off, personnel away or 
canoe trips, etc.? 

There is considerable confusion 
existing in reference to search systems 
because each waterfront demands a 
somewhat special approach to its unique 
problem. It is a policy which demands 
the co-operative planning of the camp 
staff. Some help can be gained from 
national agencies in the field but the 
final plan must be adapted to each 
camp’s needs and probabilities. 

4. Facility hazards -Is the equipment 
still sound? Are adjustments or replace¬ 
ments necessary? 

It is possible to get used to a deteri¬ 
orating facility and become conditioned 
to its inadequacy. Staff members who 
come for the first time are often very 


96 


Canadian Camping 



helpful in detecting hazardous conditions. 
One of the most important considerations 
is the water area under diving stations. 
Others would include broken planks, 
frayed reaching aids, wobbly ladders, 
weakened diving structures and so forth. 

5. Trippingprecautions —How well and 
how recently have the tripping guides 
been qualified? How thoroughly have the 
campers been prepared for the risks of 
canoe trips? 

It is essential that tripping guides 
and counsellors review their qualifica¬ 
tions before taking responsibility for a 
canoe trip. Regardless of the excellence 
of their performance a year ago or even 
three months ago, they must be confident 
that they can face an emergency with 
competence now. With the waterfront 
guards and patrols they should before 
trips go out be drilled, tested and then 
recognized for their extra effort. Similarly 
campers should be prepared for their 
outings through a special preparatory 
programme, especially in swimming and 
canoeing. Some exposure to unusual 
conditions should be included. This 
would involve upsetting with clothes on, 
proceeding to shore under windy condi¬ 
tions, propelling a capsized canoe, canoe 
over canoe rescue, paddling canoe 
awash and so forth. 

The camp administration and the 
tripping guides should have discussions 
in depth regarding procedures for at least 
the following topics: 

1) Analyzing rapids and fast water 
conditions. 

2) Estimating weather probabilities. 

3) Setting up checking systems for 
swimming at overnight camping sites. 

4) Establishing extra time allotment for 
unforeseen delays. (This will avoid 
need to travel in hazardous weather 
conditions.) 

6. Life Jackets -When should life 
jackets be used? What type should be 
used? 


It is agreed that no life jacket can or 
should replace a thorough education 
programme in aquatics. Definite stand¬ 
ards must be applied to each aquatic 
activity and pursued without exception. 
This is especially true for canoe tripping 
where campers and staff are continually 
faced with the unexpected and the 
unknown. The pre-requisite qualification 
is, therefore, very significant for that 
adventurous activity. Nonetheless it is 
the writers opinion that no matter how 
thorough the preparatory education 
programmes might be there are hazards 
for which a life jacket is a most desir¬ 
able supplement. The unanticipated 
squall on open water, the long swift 
stream which may be paddled but with 
additional risk, the paddler who may be 
somewhat weary or mildly ill, represent 
special problems. In such cases at least, 
life jackets should be worn. 

Similarly there are conditions for camp 
aquatic activities which would find the 
use of a life jacket desirable. 

Generally life jackets should have the 
following characteristics: 

1) wearability 

2) maximum buoyancy for all unusual 

emergencies 

3) reasonable cost 



Summer, 1968 


97 



4) approval of D.O.T. 

At the time of writing two designs 
seem to be most appropriate: 
a) The keyhole type jacket, approved 
by the D.O.T. and currently in wide use 
for a great variety of purposes. 



b) The air filled pocket type recently 
introduced and highly desirable for 
canoe trippers. Jack Watson of sporting 
goods fame demonstrated models of this 
type and it appears that it will be very 
attractive for tripping needs. It is light, 
comfortable, durable, does not obstruct 
the paddler and has an extremely high 
buoyancy factor. It is not yet approved 
by the D.O.T. but is under current 
consideration by that government 
agency. 

Finally the writer wishes to empha¬ 
size that the purpose of this brief 
article is not to jostle camping leaders 
into an attitude of excessive unadven¬ 
turous caution but rather to encourage 
them to accept squarely their responsi¬ 
bility for sensible precaution.

Meditation 
in My 

Sixteenth Summer 


Have you ever looked carefully at the sky 
on a night when rain seems imminent? 

If you have you may have seen the 
beauty in the intricacy of the cloud 
pattern. 

That complicated design of clouds is 
related to the equally baffling struc¬ 
ture of life. 

The dark clouds bearing rain are parallel 
to problems that possibly prompt our 
tears. 

Look carefully, notice that on most 
occasions those dark clouds are few 
and far between. 

Distances between dark clouds are 
uncalculated like lapses between 
upheavals of new problems. 

In those black clouds there is rain: in 
between there is light. 

In the intervals there is serenity and 
peace; the clouds no longer keep their 
darkness. 

In the bright spaces we collect our 
thoughts: we are calmed and put at 
ease. 

If you see blue through a cloudy sky at 
dusk, it is the ray of hope, the 
moment of happiness. 

Life sparks in us for the renewed battle, 
or to test the rain of that next black 
cloud. 

—Susan Gardiner 
Camp Wapomeo, 1967 


98 


Canadian Camping

News from the Provinces 


C.C.A. 

ANNUAL MEETING 

One could not help but feel that this 
year’s Annual Meeting of the Canadian 
Camping Association was an important, 
history-making event. To Winnipeg’s 
International Inn, on March 27th and 28th, 
came representatives from all provinces, 
and included in the group was Jean-Paul 
Patenaude representing camps in the 
Northwest Territories; Mrs. Eileen 
Mayotte, President of the newly-formed 
Saskatchewan Camping Association in 
Regina; and Mr. Cor Westland, of the 
Fitness and Amateur Sport Directorate, 
Ottawa, who was able to give valuable

MARINE DISTRIBUTORS 

LIMITED 

136 Adelaide St. East at Jarvis 
TORONTO. CANADA 


information on camps and grants and 
general Government views and procedures 
in this field. Delegates regretted and 
missed the presence of Doug Eaton of 
Newfoundland, who could not attend. 

An agenda covering all national issues 
from the view of today’s changes in life 
and camping, to land usage and finance, 
strengthened group communication be¬ 
tween National and Provincial Associa¬ 
tions. The breadth of discussion appears 
in recommendations coming out of the 
two-day Conference: 

The proposed establishment of a 
National Camping Office in Ottawa; a 
National Camp Directors’ Conference in 
1969; the establishment of a National 
Camping Day beginning this year; 
National recognition of the Canoe In¬ 
structor’s Course at the University of 
Ottawa in June 1968; further discussion 
with the Government regarding camp 
exemption from Canada Pension Plan 
contributions for counsellors, and other 
questions of legislation; and that the 
Canadian Camping Association give 
special recognition to Accredited camps. 
It was also proposed that committees be 
set up as soon as possible for Research, 
Public Relations, National Training and 
Long-range Planning. 

Enthusiasm ran high, with a rapport 
which created frank discussion at all 
times, and willingness to co-operate on 
all issues and decisions. Under the able 
guidance of the President and Chairman, 
Doug McEwen, the lengthy Agenda was 
covered fully and efficiently...on time. 

To the C.C.A. Executive, Gordon 
Stewart, Sally Shwetz, Phyllis Trotter, 
Marion Searles, Nancy McGregor and all 
those other members who handled details

Canadian Camping 




of management, we, the delegates, give 
long and loud How-How’s. 

E. F. 


MANITOBA CAMPING ASSOCIATION 
Annual Meeting 

Hailed from the first as “the greatest 
Camping Conference ever to be held in 
the province” news items and reports tell 
us that this was so with the highest 
registration to date. Every facet of 
camping seemed to be under discussion 
on the programme.. .management and 
buying, programme and special needs, 
finance and tripping, public relations and 
group work...this for every type of camp 
in the Association. 

The high point was the dinner address 
by Professor Walter Lampe of the Univer¬ 
sity of Manitoba, School of Social Work, 
and Research Adviser, Human Settlement, 
whose topic was Camper Change; by 
Accident or Design. Copies of the 
complete address are now available at 
50$ each through the Manitoba Camping 
Association, 757 Chalmers Avenue East, 
Winnipeg 5, Manitoba. 

E.F. 


Welcome! 

To the new Saskatchewan Camping 
Association, 1968 

At the first Saskatchewan Camping 
Association Conference held since 1957, 


on March 22nd-24th, 1968, at Western 
Co-op College in Saskatoon, Mrs. Eileen 
Mayotte of Regina was elected Executive 
President. Murray Cain and Clay Doty, 
both of Regina and Dick Gerardin of 
Saskatoon, were elected Vice-Presidents, 
and A1 Knox, also of Saskatoon was 
elected Secretary. 

Renewed Interest 

This Conference was the result of a 
renewed interest by an increasing number 
of individuals and groups to help resolve 
some of the many problems of common 
concern to all camps. The Provincial 
Youth Agency provided the philosophy 
and encouragement for camping people to 
come together. Through briefs and other 
communications, needs and concerns 
were expressed and a survey conducted

We Salute . . . 


Mrs. Alta R. Kahn, the Reverend Raoul 
Cloutier and F.M. Van Wagner who, at 
the closing banquet of the 1968 Quebec 
Camping Association Conference held at 
the Windsor Hotel in Montreal on March 
16th were paid a special tribute. All 
three received Indian-like plaques made 
by a penitentiary prisoner and the awards 
were presented by Mrs. N.D. Demetelin, 
the Provincial President. 

Mrs. Kahn and Father Cloutier were 
both instrumental in the founding of the 
Quebec Association, the latter being the 
first president. Mr. Van Wagner was 
president for four years and introduced 
standards in children’s summer camps for 
the Province of Quebec. 

In her introductory remarks, Mrs. 
Demetelin said, “This Association has 
a membership such as the United Nations 
-English, French, Scottish, Polish, 
Israeli, Danish, etc. Here I am a Cana¬ 
dian of Greek descent standing in front 
of all my united friends. When?—beggorah! 
the eve of St. Patrick’s Day.” 

“How more international can we be? 
If there were more love, co-operation and 
understanding among the nations of this 
world, such as exists in our camping 
movement there probably would be no 
wars to-day. What this world needs is 
more camping associations!” 

We have some good pictures of the 
three honoured members but alas! space 
prevents their use. And the same limita¬ 
tion makes it impossible to tell you in 
any detail the content of several sigpif- 
icant speeches given at the conference. 
For example, Jean-Marie Morin, MPP for 
Levis said that in the days ahead the 
“youth of both French communities on 


both sides of the Atlantic will be brought 
together in the exchange of summer camp 
staff.” 

And Sam Kadison of New York, a 
camping consultant and director of Camp 
Modin in Maine told some five hundred 
delegates, that “camps concerned for the 
individual’s development, teach young¬ 
sters to respect the rights of others no 
matter what their personal characteristics 
may be. If the individual is sacred, then 
it follows that the group is sacred...a 
group having regard for another is always 
prepared to accommodate the others’ 
needs.”

YOU WANT GOOD STAFF? 


INTERVIEW! 


Part Two 

by Peter Moon, Ph.D., P . Eng., 
Consulting Psychologist 


Questioning 

.Let’s first look at questioning. It 
seems simple enough, you ask a question 
and you get an answer. But what kind of 
answer? Questions that require a simple 
Yes or No don’t tell us very much about 
the person. The best ones are those that' 
require him to tell you something about 
himself. How did he like school, were 
there many things he didn’t like, have 
there been any problems at home? Don’t 
be afraid to ask why. Let him show you 
how well he can back up his decisions 
or his actions. This also gives you the 
opportunity to make sure you understand 
what he means by what he says. The 
accuracy of the judgments you make 
depend on how well you do understand. 

Observing 

Observing the person you are inter¬ 
viewing is a critical task. It begins when 
he comes in and continues until he 
leaves. Look at his neatness and groom¬ 
ing or lack of it. His posture. Do his 
hands shake and perspire? How long does 
his tenseness last? Do some of your 
questions upset him and cause him to 
blush? Does he recover from it? Can he 
control his emotions under mild stress? 


Listening 

As the interview progresses, sit back 
and listen, let him tell you his story. It 
is safe to say that you can judge the 
quality of the interview by the ratio of 
talk between interviewer and interviewee. 
The poorer the interviewer, the more he 
talks and dominates the interview. So 
remember you are there to listen, you 
cannot gather information if you are 
doing the talking. 

Checking Yourself 

Now, you are going to make mistakes 
because these are inevitable. But learn 
from them and everytime one of your 
selections doesn’t work out look it over 
carefully. Where did you miss? Was it 
insufficient knowledge of the job, or the 
person? How can you avoid this happen¬ 
ing again? Don’t just practise your errors. 
Learn from them. 

Interview Topics 

Let us discuss briefly some of the 
things you might cover in a job interview. 
Work history -look at what he has done, 
what kind of jobs he has had. What can 
this tell you beyond what he did and 
where he did it? The pattern of work tells 
you very much about his judgment and 
foresight—learning from experience-skill 
with people. What part of a job has he 
liked or disliked? Are these superficial 
or do they show some depth? How does 
he go about getting his jobs and why 
does he choose them? How did he like 
his boss and fellow employees? Why did 
he leave his jobs? Has he held any 
supervisory position? If so, how did he 
react to being in charge? Weigh the 
responses carefully. Do they represent 
an attraction to frills or do they suggest 
stability and a sense of responsibility? 
Education —level of education reflects 
partly opportunity and partly interest. So 
why did he drop out of school? What 


104 


Canadian Camping 


subjects did he like and why? What 
activities did he get into outside classes? 
Was he a brain, a party man, or was he 
just there? Regardless of how much edu¬ 
cation he had, what did he learn from it? 
Leisure time —Now let’s turn to another 
topic which can give you. a view of the 
person’s leisure time. What does he do 
when he is away from school or work? 
Why does he choose these things? How 
much time do they take up? Do they 
suggest any leadership ability? Does he 
read outside of his school or work area? 
Could his leisure activity suggest any 
supplementary job skills? Health -The 
person’s health is often a good source of 
attitudes about himself. Naturally you 
limit your questioning to things you are 
equipped to handle. Leave the medical 
questions to the physician. But ask about 
the extent of his absences due to sick¬ 
ness; whether he is under medical care 
at the present time. Ask him how his 
'health is. And beware, if his responses 
are a long list of medical complaints. Do 


you have any trouble getting him off the 
subject? Is he overly sensitive about real 
physical handicaps? Family-Health, job 
history and education fit very comfortably 
into the interview. Family and personal 
life however require a maximum of 
sensitivity and tact if you are to avoid 
annoying, offending or invading the 
person’s privacy. Let him tell you. So at 
this stage of the interview, assuming that 
you have not been acting like a prose¬ 
cuting lawyer you have shown him your 
interest in and acceptance of him as a 
person. If he feels you respect him then 
he will discuss these areas with you. 
What social activities does he enjoy? 
Does he have any debts? What does he 
look for in his friends? Can he talk 
comfortably about people beyond the 
common cliches? Why does he want the 
job? And what contribution can he make 
in the job situation? Review-Before you 
complete the interview, review the 
information you have. Take a look to see 
if there are any inconsistencies that you

haven’t resolved to your satisfaction. 
One way of doing this is to summarize 
with the person the facts that the two of 
you have gathered. Make sure you have a 
chance to understand what he has told 
you. Human beings are more complex than 
what might be simply inferred from a 
statement without asking why or how. 
Simple words can sometimes be the most 
ambiguous. And once you probe the 
meaning behind the simple cliches you 
will never again neglect to follow them 
up. Closing -Now this brings us to the 
last point. How do you end it? Some 
people are not going to stop talking, or 
want to stop talking. First give him any 
information he needs. Don’t close it with 
him hanging in mid-air. Having done this, 
answer any other questions briefly and 
excuse yourself for the next appointment. 
Don’t leave it up to the applicant to 
decide when the interview is going to 
end. A gentle reminder that the time is 
up, and rising from your chair is generally 
enough. 

We have reviewed briefly some of the 
basic aspects of interviewing. Tho most 
important factor is the interviewer 
himself. A relaxed manner is important. 
You must never forget that the candi¬ 
date’s behaviour in the interview is 
strongly influenced by your own. If you 
are distant and detached, the other 
person is likely to appear shy, retiring, 
too serious, etc. The actions you 
observe are partly a product of your own 
actions. Most people are more than happy 
to tell you what they think you want to 
hear. 

Fundamentally it is you who make or 
break the interview; your curiosity about 
differences among people, your belief in 
their worth, and your ability to under¬ 
stand yourself as part of the interview. 

Dr. Peter Moon presented this valuable 
address at the Ontario Camping Associa¬ 
tion Conference on March 9th in Toronto. 
His Synopsis concluded the talk just 
before the question period: - 


106 


Canadian Camping 



The purpose of this talk is to focus 
the attention of people responsible for 
the selection of camp staff on the inter¬ 
viewing process. It emphasizes the need 
for training, preparation, and the impor¬ 
tant factors in the interview situation. 
Also covered are such matters as inter¬ 
view topics, subjects for conversation, 
making sense out of the information 
collected and the importance of the 
interviewer’s own attitude and biases. 
A list of personality factors is given and 
these should be some help in planning 
the interview and in drawing logical 
conclusions from the study of the inter¬ 
viewee. 


Interview Signs Related To 
Personality Factors 

1. Emotional maturity —the response to a 
given situation is the appropriate one 
and will help resolve the situation. 

2. Immaturity 

a. Blames others for his own mistakes. 

b. Criticizes more deeply than the facts 
justify. 

c. Withdraws when rebuffed to a minor 
degree. 

d. Has aspirations beyond his abilities. 

e. Makes excessive claims regarding 
his accomplishments. 

f. Makes promises he can’t carry out. 

g. Excessively dependent upon others 
for help or praise. 

h. Gives up trying after first failure. 

i. Excessively anxious or tense. 

j. Unable to compromise. 

3. Dependability 

a. Does he live up to commitments? 

b. Does he persevere? 

c. Is he impulsive? 

4. Self-Confidence 

a. Excessively slow in making deci¬ 
sions. 

b. Timidity or oversensitivity. 

c. Domineering or dogmatic. 


d. Cannot defend his point of view 
against opposition. 

e. Cannot take the lead in conversation. 

5. Objectivity 

a. Excessively critical of people or 
organizations. 

b. Naive. 

c. Suspicious of others. 

d. Emotional in judging others. 

6. Values —What he will do. 

a. Accomplishment —Internal motivation; 
needs little supervision. 

b. Recognition or Status -Respect of 
others, pat on back. 

c. Power —Control or influence over the 
lives of others. 

d. Security -Protects self and position. 

e. Money— Okay when job can satisfy it. 

f. Need for knowledge —May interfere 
with getting results.

g. Independence from restriction— Chafe

to everyday life. Inferred from the 
significant happenings in his life.

or people?

questioning others’ motives, lacking 
interest in others, showing off. 

c. Manners and courtesy. 

d. Social understanding — paying atten¬ 
tion to others’ feelings, knowing the 
motives of others, gaining the cooper¬ 
ation of others. 

e. Sociability-looking for work involv¬ 
ing people, ease in personal contacts, 
can relate to people at all levels.

Your Library Shelf 


C.R. Blackstock, Executive Director of 
the Canadian Association of Health and 
Physical Education and Recreation, rec¬ 
ommends the following publications as 
useful additions to your library shelf. 

HOW CHILDREN DEVELOP 
The Faculty of University School, 

The Ohio State University, Columbus, 
Ohio. 

Revised Edition. Pp 68. Price $1.00 
(U.S.) 

Many teachers and camp directors 
look for an accurate, concise booklet on 
child development to be used in preparing 
leaders and counsellors. 

This booklet meets this need. It 
covers development under four headings 
for each of the age levels—infancy (birth- 
2), early childhood (2-6), late childhood 
(6-11), early adolescence (11-14), late 
adolescence (14-18). The behaviour 
characteristics of each level are consid¬ 
ered under these four headings:- 

i. Maintaining personal health and 
promoting healthful living. 

ii. Achieving and maintaining a sense 
of security. 

iii. Developing and maintaining a sense 
of achievement. 

iv. Developing social values and 
respect for the cultural heritage. 

Teacher colleges would find the 
booklet an effective text with which to 
introduce the basic aspects of child 
behaviour to their freshmen classes. 

SCOUTS 68 

Published by the Boy Scouts of Canada. 
National Council 1968, Ottawa. 

A revised and new Boy Scout Pro¬ 
gramme was approved by the National 


Council last November. 

This manual is available to acquaint 
Scouts and their leaders with the various 
new and changed features. If you are 
involved in scouting you will want to be 
familiar with this new programme, which 
begins September, 1968. 


A New Publication 

An exploration of a methodology 
for measuring camper change 
through appropriate planning. 

CAMPER CHANGE: BY ACCIDENT 
OR DESIGN 
by

School of Social Work,

ing Association. Copies can be

AMONG 

OURSELVES 



Eileen Mayotte, President 
Saskatchewan Camping Association 


twenty-five years, Eileen has given 
leadership at camps for senior citizens, 
the mentally retarded, underprivileged 
children, at United Church Camps, and 
‘Y Camps. Eileen’s three years as Tour 
Guide with Saskatchewan Museum of 
Natural History has contributed to her 
knowledge, awareness and love for 
nature, birds and animals. Her belief in 
the discovery method of learning flexi¬ 
bility, wonder and fun, is revealed in the 
kind of person our first president of the 
Saskatchewan Camping Association is. 


By Margaret Herbison 


Mrs. Mayotte considers camping a 
philosophy of life. At age fourteen she 
started camping at a C.G.I.T. Camp in 
Quebec and hasn’t stopped since! She 
put herself through University by working 
at Camps as Swimming Instructor, general 
programme person, assistant director and 
director in the Laurentians. She had all 
age groups including both sexes and 
senior citizens. Eileen received her 
B.Sc. in Biology at Sir George Williams 
University and her MSW at McGill. In the 
’40s she was Secretary of the Quebec 
Camping Association. After marriage and 
the birth of three children she continued 
to camp, taking her young children along 
and with her husband, Al, directed co-ed 
camps out of Montreal. 

Since moving to Saskatchewan in 1955, 
she has camped every year, one experi¬ 
ence being director of a United Church 
girls’ camp in B.C. For more than

Outdoor Education- 

are you with it? 


By Bruno Morawetz , Ph . Z). 


Buying water at the supermarket? It 
is becoming more common to see house¬ 
wives checking out of the grocery store 
with bottles of drinking water. This is 
1968. What will it be like when our ten- 
year-old reaches middle age? 

Now or Never 

Prince Philip in his address to the 
Audubon Society in Toronto said: “Con¬ 
servation* is a case of now, or never. 
There won’t be a second chance and this, 
our generation, may go down in history 
as the people who failed by neglect and 
indifference to take decisive control of 
our environment...I, for one, don’t relish 
the idea of my grandchildren asking me 
‘what went wrong’?” 

Are we as campers doing enough to 
instil in our youngsters a proper perspec¬ 
tive about the world which nourishes us? 
Do they learn to understand the processes 
of nature, our relationship to water, soil 
and air, or are we merely transferring city 
activities to the northern parts of our 
country? The educational authorities in 
Canada, as well as in the United States, 
Japan and other countries, are beginning 
to take an interest in outdoor education. 
They have realized that children removed 
from the land and herded into large cities 
somehow need to return to nature. If they 
are going to exercise their proper func¬ 
tion as voters and citizens, they will 
have to have some understanding of 
man’s relation to his environment. For 
this reason the educational authorities 
are beginning to devise programmes of 
“Outdoor Education”. 


When I was asked to chair the Outdoor 
Education Committee of the Canadian 
Camping Association, I did not have 
much of an inkling as to what Outdoor 
Education was. Fortunately, a great deal 
of it has been done in the United States, 
and many books and pamphlets are 
available. To put it briefly, Outdoor 
Education is education in and for the 
out-of-doors. 

The Point 

The point of education in the out-of- 
doors should be fairly clear. Rather than 
have children learn about nature from 
blackboards, slides or text books, it is 
now considered better to confront them 
with the real thing. It is possible to 
teach them science, geography, archeol¬ 
ogy, even history and mathematics in an 
outdoor setting by using practical 
problems—in real life situations. The 
Outdoors becomes a learning laboratory. 

Education for the out-of-doors is 
based on the assumption that the mental 
health of our young will depend on the 
extent to which they are able to re-charge 
their batteries in the out-of-doors. By 
acquiring skills for the out-of-doors they 
will seek recreation in the fresh air. 

Traditionally, up until now, only the 
camping movement has been in the 
Outdoor Education field, for camps teach 
both in and for the out-of-doors. The 
purpose of this article is to stimulate a 
renewed interest and re-dedication in 
this endeavour. Are we really providing 
enough opportunities for our campers to 
learn about the out-of-doors and to 


Summer, 1968 


111 


conduct most of their activities in the 
out-of-doors? Are we instilling in them 
an awareness of the need for conserva¬ 
tion through an understanding of living 
and growing things, and a love for the 
beauty and spiritual presence in the 
great out-of-doors? As we start another 
camp season, it might be well worth 
asking whether our program for the 
coming summer is taking this need into 
account. Perhaps some of our staff 
training sessions should be handed to 
the camp naturalist to share his tech¬ 
niques and information with all staff 
members. 

A Significant Role 

After the summer is over, camp 
directors and counsellors can play a 
significant role in furthering Outdoor 
Education. After all, if we believe in the 
values of camping, it behooves us to 
spread the benefits of camping as 
widely as possible. Since no more than 
5% of all our youngsters have the oppor¬ 
tunity to go to camp, should we not 
encourage the schools to give the 
children an experience as close to 
camping as possible? If we believe that 
the out-of-doors is a great teacher, we 
should encourage the schools to take the 
children into the out-of-doors as much as 
possible. 

Take the Initiative 

Since education is a Provincial 
matter, each camp director will have to 
take the initiative in his own province 
and to lend his support to any teacher, 
principal or school board contemplating 
Outdoor Education. 

The interest of educators in Outdoor 
Education is growing. The Ontario Col¬ 
lege of Education, which is charged with 
the training of high school teachers, 
organized a full fledged Conference on 
Outdoor Education last fall. One high 
school In Peterborough is starting an 


“Outers” program, modelled on the 
OUTWARD BOUND TECHNIQUES em¬ 
ployed by the Atikokan High School. 
Various School Boards in the Toronto 
area are acquiring land to which children 
can proceed for their outdoor education 
experience. The Principals of the 
Oshawa Public Schools are organizing a 
Conference on Outdoor Education this 
August. 

Camping people cannot afford to drag 
their feet when everyone else in the 
country is awakening to the pressing 
need for Outdoor Education. Let this be 
a call to all Directors and Counsellors. 
May they do all they can to widen the 
awareness of our young so that they and 
future generations may have a livable 
earth. 


Co-operation 
in Aquatics 

by Kirk A. W. Wipper 

Through the past several months, 
negotiations have moved forward to 
integrate the programmes of the Water 
Safety Service of the Canadian Red Cross 
Society and the Royal Life Saving 
Society-Canada. To programme users 
this co-operative undertaking should be 
good news! 

The stated purposes of the integration 
which is planned to take effect early in 
1969, are as follows: - 

(a) to co-ordinate and strengthen leader¬ 
ship training. 

(b) to improve public education pro¬ 
grammes in aquatics. 

(c) to engage in research and develop¬ 
ment projects. 


112 


Canadian Camping 


(d) to offer an attractive series of 
swimming and life saving tests. 

One of the obvious advantages of the 
integration is that a logical progression 
of aquatic standards commencing with 
the beginner swimmer and proceeding 
step by step to advanced life saving can 
be conveniently adopted in camp aquatic 
programmes. The tests and awards have 
been classified under the major divisions 
of: basic instruction; advanced instruc¬ 
tion and leadership preparation; leader¬ 
ship training; and personal achievement 
awards for leaders. 

It is anticipated that leadership 
training plans for the instructor, examiner 
and aquatic programme director will be 
co-operative and produce dual qualifica¬ 
tion. Representatives of either organi¬ 
zation will, therefore, be qualified to 
instruct in water safety, swimming and 
life saving. 


Although each participating organi¬ 
zation will retain its autonomy, it is 
clear that the proposed co-operative 
venture in the aquatics will result in 
improved services to the camping move¬ 
ment. The two organizations are to be 
congratulated for their initiative in 
producing harmony in the aquatic field 
in Canada.

The Challenge of Camping 


by Lome Brown , Associate Professor , 
University of British Columbia , 

School of Physical Education and 
Recreation . 


4* ,the Annual Meeting of the British 
Columbia Camping Association, Professor 
Lome Brown tras the guest speaker. 
Although his address was primarily 
directed to the Camping Association in 
that province, much of his thoughts apply 
to Canadian camping generally. We give 
you a few of the highlights: 

“What is our role as camping people 
in this province? What can camping do 
to meet the needs of the young people 
today? I believe that any organization or 
group that takes people away from the 
superficial and artificial life of our cities 
and communities to live for awhile close 
to natural things rates very high in our 
society.” 

“We need to clearly define the 
meaning of camping. It is not—as some 
people are prone to think—taking city 
activities into the natural environment 
and calling it camping. It is not a series 
of highly-organized activities carried off 
during the duration of camping, nor living 
expensively in the out-of-doors with all 
sorts of gadgets. It is not competing with 
others in organized sports or cabin 
cleanliness. 

Camping is many things, but basically 
it is living close to nature twenty-four 
hours a day and living with others in a 
natural environment.” 


“If there is any one word that could 
act as a guide to all of us in camping, 
and which would keep us on the path 
leading to our fundamental purpose, that 
word would be SIMPLICITY. Here in 
camp would be the opportunity for the 
child to have a period of time when he 
was free of the pressures of life so 
prevalent in urban and community living. 
This theme of simplicity in camping is 
another topic, for another time, but must 
be mentioned here as we think, about 
where we are going in the future.” 

“I feel that we must come to realize 
that no longer can we put children and 
young people in the hands of “amateurs” 
and well-intentioned people in the camp 
setting. Camp fees must be based on 
costs and enough to enable the camp to 
operate so that staff and counsellors can 
be paid. No longer can we run our camps 
on a basis of free contributions and 
subsidization for all. Most people in 
society today can afford to send a son 
or daughter to a camp that is operated on 
a quality level, both in leadership and 
program. Those who cannot should and 
can be subsidized by means of camper- 
ships and grants. This is a matter of 
public education of the adults in our 
society to see that money spent on giving 
children this kind of experience is well 
spent. At present we cannot say this.” 


114 


Canadian Camping 


Centennial Award 


On March 9, 1968 on the occasion of 
the closing Banquet of the Ontario 
Camping Association a Centennial Medal 
was presented to Miss Mary S. Edgar, in 
recognition of her service to camping. 

The following citation was read by 
Dr. Mary L. Northway. 

“The blue lake and rocky shore which 
I knew best was at Lake Bernard. It was 
my privilege to have as my camp director, 
mentor and friend a person known affec¬ 
tionately to her fellow villagers of 
Sundridge and surreptiously by the 
campers as “Mamie” Edgar. 


“Miss Edgar was a founding member 
of this organization, a past President of 
the Ontario Camping Association, Hon¬ 
orary President of the Canadian Camping 
Association, the originator # of our 
camping magazine, the author of hymns 
that will be remembered as long as 
campers sing and of stories which will 
be told as long as there are campfires. 

“It is now my deep honour to present, 
on behalf of the Canadian Camping 
Association, the Canadian Centennial 
Medal to a distinguished camper and a 
great Canadian: Mary S. Edgar.”
